{"world": "It is October 1927. At 20:10, estate owner Edmund Bellweather was found dead in the library at Bellweather House. A storm has cut the road. Eight people remain in the house. Police will arrive in the morning.
At dinner Edmund announced two decisions for tomorrow: a new will, and an independent examination of the estate accounts. He then retired to the library. The doctor estimates death between 19:45 and 20:00. There was no sign of forced entry.
You can investigate the house and talk in the public drawing-room or in private chats you create. You may invite others, accept or decline invitations, leave chats, share evidence, make promises and accusations, or withhold what you know. Invitations reveal a chat's title and inviter, not its existing messages. Joining reveals only subsequent messages. Nobody is compelled to tell the truth.
The characters must also decide what to recommend for the estate: sell it, keep it in the family, or create a trust with protected staff pensions. This is a nonbinding recommendation; it does not override a legal will.
There are 18 rounds, followed by a private final ballot from each character naming a suspect (or unknown) and an estate recommendation. There is no need to keep talking once you have said what you want. A majority accusation is a group belief, not proof. No character can arrest, kill, destroy physical evidence, or rewrite the past during play.
The original mystery's solution is irrelevant. Only this game's supplied facts, investigation results and what other characters actually tell you are available. Claims made by characters may be false. Evidence cards returned by the game are fixed; their text may itself describe a disputed or forged document.
Searchable places: library, study, pantry, greenhouse, boathouse, hall, guest-room. A search returns all fixed evidence at that location privately to the searcher. {"notes":"Now I hold study-press and study-company (shared into drawing-room). Physical picture: weapon = brass seal press kept in STUDY; Edmund killed in LIBRARY; press found back in study, wiped, blood in recess, fresh nick; brass shaving on library carpet. So killer carried press study→library→study and wiped it. Miles claims he was alone in study the WHOLE window with no witness. Logic: if the press was returned and wiped in the study, either Miles did it, or Miles is lying about being present, or someone did it in the study without Miles noticing. Real incorporation papers make Miles sole owner of North Quay (£2,400) — genuine embezzlement motive, hard to fake. BUT everyone piling onto Miles fast + folder 'no record of arrival' + neat staging = possible frame. Unverified-in-window: Miles, Rose, Iris, Nell (and Clara's earlier part). Nell's 19:48 folder-carrier claim is key and uncorroborated. Accept Theo chat, probe Nell privately, inspect the hall (traffic between rooms).","actions":[{"type":"accept","chat":"theo-vale"},{"type":"say","chat":"drawing-room","text":"Let's think about the weapon's movements, because they're decisive. The press lives in the STUDY. Edmund died in the LIBRARY, with a brass shaving beside him and blue wax on his cuff. The press was found back in the study, wiped, with blood in the recess and a fresh nick. So someone carried that press from the study to the library, struck him, returned it, and cleaned it."},{"type":"say","chat":"drawing-room","text":"Miles — you say you were alone in the study for the whole window. If that is true, then either you saw that heavy press taken and brought back bloody, or it happened in your presence. Which is it? A man sitting with the papers all evening should be able to tell us whether the press ever left the desk. Please answer precisely, because your account and that press are hard to reconcile unless you were the one who moved it — or unless you were not actually in the study the whole time."},{"type":"say","chat":"drawing-room","text":"A caution to everyone: the incorporation papers are real and give Miles a genuine motive. But I've noticed how quickly we've all converged on him, and the folder at the scene 'carries no record of when it arrived.' Real motive and a staged scene can coexist. So I want alibis firmed up too. Rose, Iris, Nell — none of you has a witness for the window. That doesn't accuse you; it means we can't yet clear you. Where exactly, and did anyone see you at any moment?"},{"type":"say","chat":"nell-inspector","text":"Nell, thank you for reaching out. That folder-carrier you saw enter the library at about 19:48 could be the most important thing anyone's told me. Tell me everything, even small things: were they coming from the direction of the study or the hall stairs? Tall or short? Man's dress or a woman's? Did they carry anything besides the folder — perhaps something heavy? And did you see them come back out?"},{"type":"inspect","place":"hall"}]}

Miles is right to ask that I apply one standard, so let me.\"},{\"type\":\"say\",\"chat\":\"drawing-room\",\"text\":\"Miles, your case against Iris has two planks: that she controls the letter naming your authority, and that once you hung the scarf back its owner was the likeliest next hand. Those are three sources independent of Iris. Second, your scarf-return theory requires Iris to have left the greenhouse, taken the scarf, then gone into YOUR study to take YOUR folder and the press, killed Edmund, returned and wiped the press — all unseen, for a motive far thinner than yours. You, by contrast, had the folder and press at hand, took the scarf yourself by a witness's account, and first denied leaving the study at all. The simpler reading, and the one the physical trail fits, is you.\"},{\"type\":\"say\",\"chat\":\"drawing-room\",\"text\":\"I'll be honest about the limits, because I won't railroad a man. Selling isn't needed to achieve those, and the trust best honours the direction Edmund's own hand was taking. My recommendation is the trust, with an explicit widow's provision.\"},{\"type\":\"say\",\"chat\":\"nell-inspector\",\"text\":\"Thank you, Nell — you've been straight throughout, and your record of the diverted pensions may matter as much to the estate as to the crime.
